prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, opening a new regime of precision measurement and tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Having read the other seven ballots, I move B036 from seventh to first. Four of the six members who ranked it placed it in their top three, and the arguments are ones I find persuasive from a device-physics standpoint. The magic-wavelength idea removes the trap-induced light shift as the limiting systematic, and the lattice clock then becomes a controllable many-body quantum system whose uncertainty reaches the 10^-18 level. This is a clean, reproduced demonstration that a basic quantum phenomenon can be made visible and controllable to extraordinary precision, which is the kind of result I value. It has been confirmed independently in several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), with clock comparisons over fibre and free space, which answers my usual question about robustness and reproducibility across groups. The two-name credit (Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking it to record stability and systematic control) is compact and defensible, and the science is mature and stable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one that made me rank it low at the outset: frequency combs (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion-trap clocks (Wineland, 2012) have already been honoured, so it can be read as an extension of rewarded metrology rather than a new regime of physics. The history of early lattice-clock priority (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Ye and the magic-wavelength theory) is also not settled by the supplied names, and the pending redefinition of the second could make the case clearer if the committee chose to wait. I also lean on colleagues in atomic physics for the finer credit history; this is outside my own specialty.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B036 first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique opening new ways of observing nature, while noting that the committee might wait for the SI second redefinition and that comb and ion-clock recognition could be read as overlap.
responses.response: I now agree with Kroll on the merits, and that is why I changed my ranking. I disagree mildly that waiting is attractive: the performance is already independently reproduced, and the Nobel criterion is the discovery or invention, not the legal redefinition of the second. Prize timing should not be tied to a metrology committee's schedule. On B007 I note Kroll's declared conflict as a quantum-memory practitioner, which is a reason to treat his second place there with some care, and I would still say the compound light-matter interface topic needs a sharper citable discovery than it has now.

responses.point: Lindroth sees the lattice clock as atomic structure and light-shift theory turned into an instrument with very clear fundamental content, with a clean two-person credit, and asks whether the ion-clock lineage or comb contributors need sharing.
responses.response: Her framing is the one that moved me: the magic-wavelength condition is a precise statement about atomic polarisabilities, and the instrument's accuracy follows from it. I disagree that the ion-clock lineage needs sharing, since Wineland's 2012 prize concerned quantum control of single ions and the lattice clock is a distinct many-atom scheme. I do agree that the citation should be built around the lattice concept to avoid reopening the comb and ion-clock credit. On B017 we both note that the three-name limit makes a collaboration prize hard, and I defer to the particle physicists.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a decisive instrument advance with overwhelming independent confirmation, and ranks B036 second; she also flags her own bias as a microscopist and the Urban attribution problem.
responses.response: I agree with her on B036 and accept that instrument-led prizes are legitimate when they open new measurement regimes. On B021 I qualify: I find the impact strong, but I am less sure it is physics rather than engineering, and the open attribution (Urban versus Rose, Haider and Krivanek) would need archival checking before I could support it. I am outside this field and defer to her on instrumentation details, but I would not put it above the clock.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle graphene first, as a model-first discovery whose flat-band mechanism was quantitatively tested and opened moire quantum matter, and argues the discovery is mature enough despite the unresolved superconducting pairing.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism is elegant and I agree the physics is original. Our disagreement is on maturity: I ranked it eighth because the discovery dates only from 2018, the pairing mechanism is open, and twist-angle disorder limits sample-to-sample reproducibility, which is exactly the robustness question I care about. I keep it as an alternative, but I take his point that the flat-band picture itself is stable.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a window on the universe built over decades, and ranks the Higgs experiments second, while admitting that large-collaboration credit and the many pioneers make the allocation delicate.
responses.response: I defer to him on astroparticle physics, and I agree the diffuse flux is a real discovery. My reservation is the one he raises himself: source identification rests largely on IceCube alone and the statistics for TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are moderate, so I would want independent confirmation before giving it first place. I also doubt that Halzen and Spiering represent the DUMAND, AMANDA and Baikal lineage fairly, which makes B012 harder to defend than the lattice clock.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks time-reversal-invariant topological insulators first as a conceptual surprise, a new classification of phases tied to measured transport, and acknowledges that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator work are not credited.
responses.response: I share his admiration of the Kane-Mele Z2 idea and ranked it sixth for that reason. The credit problem he lists is, in my view, decisive for this particular trio: omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from a prize that rests on the HgTe observation weakens the theory-experiment pairing, and the 2016 topological-phases prize already covered conceptual ground. I would not support B054 without a revised credit list.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views lattice clocks as a sufficiently distinct step beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
The early priority history among lattice-clock groups (Katori, Ye, Lemonde and others) beyond the two supplied names.

Whether B044 (circuit QED) is too close to the 2025 circuit prize, and whether Wallraff's omission from the credited names can be repaired, which is why I keep it as an alternative and not my first choice.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will be seen as premature given the unresolved pairing mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a close colleague of groups in superconducting circuits. My opening first place (B044, circuit QED) is in my own field, and Chalmers hosted 2025 circuit laureates as guest researchers, so I would recuse myself from deciding on B044 if it advanced. For B036 (lattice clocks), no specific conflict is apparent from my profile.
